MX-like Tensor Core for LLM Inference with NPU Integration via Hardware-Software Co-Design Exploration

Conference: 32nd Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference; January 25–28, 2027; Tokyo, Japan32nd Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASPDAC ’27), January 25–28, 2027, Tokyo, JapanDOI: 10.1145/3840404.3848173ISBN: 979-8-4007-2923-2/2027/01CCS: Hardware Arithmetic and datapath circuitsCCS: Hardware Hardware-software codesignCCS: Computer systems organization Neural networks

Abstract.

Block-scaled quantization formats such as OCP Microscaling (MX) and NVFP4 have been widely adopted as efficient data formats for LLM inference. However, the design space of these formats spanned by shared scale, weight, and activation format combinations has not been systematically explored, and the joint accuracy–silicon tradeoff across this space remains uncharacterized, leaving the true Pareto-optimal configurations for NPU-based edge LLM deployment an open question. To bridge this gap, we conduct a joint hardware–software (HW–SW) co-design exploration of the above underexplored MX-like design space with three innovations. 1) We define and systematically characterize the full 8-bit scale format family within the MX-like design space, jointly with asymmetric weight-activation precision, identifying configurations that outperform the MX and NVFP4-like (without per-tensor scaling, PTS) baselines. 2) We build a per-format specialized MAC datapath template that enables fair hardware cost evaluation across the space. 3) We develop an automated co-design flow, integrated into the open-source SNAX NPU platform, that enables joint HW-SW analysis across the design space. Overall, our co-design exploration reveals that scale format matters only under aggressive FP4 quantization, yielding a case-oriented design guideline for both scale format and asymmetric weight-activation precision. We further identify UE5M3 as a favorable accuracy–hardware tradeoff for the FP4 regime, reducing perplexity degradation by up to 25.3% relative to the NVFP4-like baseline, at a cost of only +0.06+0.06% area and +0.49+0.49% power overhead.

Keywords: 
Microscaling (MX), block-scaled quantization, LLM inference, NPU, hardware-software co-design, design space exploration

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, from natural language understanding to code generation (Grattafiori et al., 2024). However, this growing capability comes with a corresponding growth in model size (Bahri et al., 2024), demanding ever more memory and computational resources. This makes efficient LLM deployment a significant challenge, an issue that becomes even more pressing when deployment targets shift from datacenter GPUs (Ma and Patterson, 2026) toward edge NPUs (Zheng et al., 2025).

Block-scaled quantization (Dai et al., 2021; Rouhani et al., 2023c; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025) addresses this by quantizing small groups within the tensor and assigning a shared scale to each group to accommodate its local distribution. This allows high-precision values to be stored and computed in low-bitwidth datatypes, reducing memory footprint and power consumption while preserving accuracy. As shown in Fig. 1, the OCP MX (Rouhani et al., 2023a) specification and NVIDIA’s NVFP4 (NVIDIA et al., 2025) mark two industry endpoints in the resulting accuracy-hardware tradeoff. MX adopts an unsigned power-of-two block scale (UE8M0) for its prime hardware efficiency, while NVFP4 instead adopts a fractional UE4M3 block scale to improve quantization granularity.

However, MX and NVFP4 each commit to a single point in the scale format space, UE8M0 and UE4M3, respectively. On the algorithmic side, prior works (Rouhani et al., 2023c; Fasoli et al., 2026) have only explored a small part of the MX-like design space in Fig. 1: (Rouhani et al., 2023c) sweeps element formats across INT8, FP8, FP6, and FP4 but fixes the scale format to E8M0, while (Fasoli et al., 2026) explores fractional scale formats but restricts the analysis to FP4, leaving the joint interaction between scale format and element format not yet fully characterized. This uncertainty is compounded by a further consideration: activation and weight tensors exhibit different distributions (Xiao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024). Activations are heavy-tailed with significant outliers, whereas weights follow a near-Gaussian profile, suggesting that asymmetric weight-activation configurations could be beneficial. Such asymmetry has mainly been studied in weight-only quantization at per-tensor and per-token granularity (Xiao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024), but with limited attention in the block-scaled setting.

On the hardware side, the silicon cost surface over the MX-like format space remains unquantified. Prior MX-compatible MAC datapaths fix the scale to UE8M0 with symmetric (activation, weight) operands, either as a single FP8 implementation (İslamoğlu et al., 2025; Lutz et al., 2024) or as a runtime precision-scalable unit that reuses the hardware for all MX element formats (Cuyckens et al., 2025; Cuyckens et al., 2026), making the intrinsic cost of one format combination unobservable. Besides, fractional scales introduce a scale-mantissa multiplier and the operand pairs change the datapath width throughout the whole datapath, which couples the cost of one format axis to the other two. Measuring this space fairly requires a per-format combination datapath under one uniform micro-architecture.

Moreover, the above two gaps are not independent. Examining accuracy and hardware cost in isolation is insufficient, since a format that excels on one may be suboptimal on the other. Algorithmic studies (Fasoli et al., 2026; Rouhani et al., 2023c) treat hardware cost with varying and often limited rigor rather than systematic silicon evaluation, while prior hardware designs (Cuyckens et al., 2026; İslamoğlu et al., 2025) characterize silicon cost for a fixed format. As a result, the joint accuracy-silicon Pareto frontier for edge NPU deployment remains unmapped.

In this work, as shown in Fig. 1(left), we address these gaps with a joint hardware–software (HW–SW) co-design exploration of the MX-like design space, spanned by the scale, weight, and activation formats, that lies between MX and NVFP4. To fairly expose the cost of each format combination despite the coupling across format axes, we build a per-format specialized datapath under one uniform micro-architecture, and integrate it into an automated flow for joint accuracy-silicon analysis targeting edge NPU deployment. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    MX-like design space characterization: We identify a previously overlooked region within the MX-like design space, spanning intermediate scale formats and asymmetric weight-activation precision, and systematically characterize it to reveal configurations that outperform both the MX and the NVFP4-like baselines.

  • •

    Parameterized MAC datapath template: We design a parameterized template for an MX-compatible datapath to support MX-like format combinations and evaluate the variation of hardware cost across the design space.

  • •

    Automated co-design flow: We provide an automated end-to-end flow encompassing hardware generation, system integration, and numerical verification, enabling efficient design space exploration (DSE) and HW-SW co-analysis that identifies practical configurations under application-specific accuracy and hardware budget constraints.

After constructing the Pareto front for hardware efficiency and software accuracy, we find that the UE8M0 scale is preferred above A6W6 while the UE5M3 scale dominates FP4 quantization, with asymmetric configurations and narrow-exponent element formats offering further gains. Together, these findings provide case-oriented guidelines for selecting block-scaled quantization configurations under application-specific accuracy and hardware constraints.

2. BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION

Table 1 positions our work against the prior works along the five axes that reveal the gap. To the best of our knowledge, no prior art spans all five. We elaborate on the following aspects.

Quantization algorithms for LLMs: Recent algorithmic studies refine the block-scaled recipe in two directions. The first direction tunes the scale format itself.  (Chmiel et al., 2025) sweeps over FP8-typed scales in FP4 training and identifies fractional E4M3 scales as the accuracy optimum. Fasoli et al. (Fasoli et al., 2026) propose UE5M3 scale for FP4 inference. The second direction diversifies the representation. Per-block schemes such as AMXFP4 (Lee et al., 2025) and BlockDialect (Jang and Tambe, 2025) establish the value of asymmetric, block-specific formats. The strongest hardware evidence in this line consists of spot checks of one proposal against one baseline: a single-point area comparison of UE5M3 scale logic (Fasoli et al., 2026), a MAC synthesis placing AMXFP4 about 10% over MXFP4 (Lee et al., 2025), and a MAC-level match against FP4 (Jang and Tambe, 2025). None of these studies map how cost varies across the scale family, how it couples with the element formats, or whether the FP4-regime findings hold at higher precision, motivating our extension of the design space.

MX-compatible MAC and tensor core: Hardware support for block-scaled formats follows three strategies. 1) Fixed-function units implement one format well. Examples include a fused FP8 dot product unit (Lutz et al., 2024) and an ISA extension on the Snitch cluster (İslamoğlu et al., 2025). 2) Runtime hardware-reuse makes the datapath precision-scalable: sub-word parallelism reuses the 2-bit multipliers and adders across all six MX element formats (Cuyckens et al., 2026; Cuyckens et al., 2025). 3) Runtime replication instead carries parallel units for each supported pair. FGMP (Hooper et al., 2025) places four dot-product units per lane to mix FP4 and FP8 blocks, at 3.5×\times the datapath area of a single-format unit. These designs (Lutz et al., 2024; İslamoğlu et al., 2025; Cuyckens et al., 2026; Cuyckens et al., 2025; Hooper et al., 2025) differ in how they trade efficiency for format coverage, but they leave the same two dimensions untouched. Each fixes the block scale to a single format, UE8M0 or UE4M3, and none supports fully asymmetric operation analysis. As a result, prior designs cannot realize or evaluate the broader scale-format and asymmetric space explored in this work, which motivates a datapath template specialized per configuration to expose the hardware cost of each one.

Joint accuracy-silicon exploration: Joint exploration of accuracy and silicon cost has been applied to several axes of the quantization design space. A few works co-explore accuracy and silicon cost, each along one axis: quantization bit-widths in VS-Quant (Dai et al., 2021), block-scaling structure in shared microexponents (Rouhani et al., 2023b) which seeded the MX standard (Rouhani et al., 2023a), and number systems with MAC parameters in a recent sweep (Crafton et al., 2025). None of these studies varies the exponent-mantissa split of the block scale format itself, nor pairs it with a full range of asymmetric weight-activation operands.

3. Design space exploration

3.1. MX-like Design Space Characterization

We define the MX-like design space over the full 8-bit scale format family, paired with symmetric and asymmetric weight-activation precision. Unlike NVFP4’s UE4M3 scale, which leaves its sign bit permanently unused for FP8 alignment, this family reallocates every bit to exponent range or mantissa precision, and we characterize its accuracy landscape to identify practical configurations.

The element formats evaluated, FP4 E2M1, FP6 E2M3/E3M2, FP8 E4M3/E5M2, and MXINT8, follow the OCP Microscaling (MX) specification (Rouhani et al., 2023a), spanning precisions from 8 bits down to 4 bits, the range most relevant to edge deployment. The block scale format family is parameterized as UEeeMmm, with ee exponent bits and mm mantissa bits (e+m=8e+m=8), decoded as:

(1) S={2eb−bias​(1+mb/2m)eb>021−bias⋅mb/2meb=0,bias=2e−1−1.S=\begin{cases}2^{e_{b}-\mathrm{bias}}\!\left(1+m_{b}/2^{m}\right)&e_{b}>0\\ 2^{1-\mathrm{bias}}\cdot m_{b}/2^{m}&e_{b}=0\end{cases},\quad\mathrm{bias}=2^{e-1}-1.

For UE8M0 (m=0m=0), finite scales are decoded as S=2eb−127S=2^{e_{b}-127} for eb∈{0,…,254}e_{b}\in\{0,\ldots,254\}. The encoding eb=255e_{b}=255 is reserved for NaN, as defined in (Rouhani et al., 2023a). The search space spans UE8M0 to UE0M8, with UE4M3 additionally included to enable direct comparison with NVFP4. For each scale format, the block scale factor is computed as S=max⁡|x|/QmaxS=\max|x|/Q_{\max} with round-up, following the block-scaled quantization procedure adopted in recent MX training and inference recipes (Mishra et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2025), where QmaxQ_{\max} is the maximum representable value of the element format.

However, this design space, spanned by scale format, weight format, and activation format, is combinatorially large, making exhaustive evaluation with a rigorous experimental setup computationally prohibitive. To prune this design space to a set of practical configurations and identify clear trends within it, we characterize its accuracy landscape as shown in Fig. 2, with Qwen2.5-3B (Qwen Team, 2024) and Llama-3.2-1B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), using WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) perplexity on 30 randomly sampled sequences of 2048 tokens. All quantization uses a block size of 16 to ensure fair comparison with the NVFP4 quantization setup. To measure how quantization degrades accuracy relative to each model’s own full-precision baseline, we adopt this relative perplexity metric:

(2) ΔPPL%=PPL−PPLbasePPLbase×100%,\Delta{\mathrm{PPL}}_{\%}=\frac{\mathrm{PPL}-\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}}{\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}}\times 100\%,

where lower values indicate better accuracy retention.

The characterization yields three findings that shape the practical design space. First, the scale format’s exponent width has a hard floor. As Fig. 2(a) shows for Qwen2.5-3B, formats with fewer than 4 exponent bits (UE3M5 to UE0M8) degrade accuracy severely across most weight/activation combinations, because the scale cannot represent the activation tensor’s dynamic range. This restricts the practical scale formats from UE8M0 to UE4M4 and UE4M3, ruling out approximately half of the design space. Second, within this range, fractional scale formats such as UE5M3 and UE4M4 provide a measurable accuracy advantage over UE8M0 and NVFP4’s UE4M3, particularly in the FP4 regime. In contrast, NVFP4 additionally introduces a second-level FP32 per-tensor scale on top of its block scale (NVIDIA et al., 2025). As illustrated in Fig. 2(b), incorporating this PTS yields only marginal accuracy improvement within this range, at the cost of two additional whole-tensor memory traversals for tensor-level scaling. Since choosing a better scale format achieves a larger accuracy gain without this overhead, this work prioritizes scale format selection over per-tensor scaling. Third, asymmetric weight-activation configurations further improve accuracy over symmetric ones at the same weight precision, an effect that is most pronounced in the FP4 regime, as depicted in Fig. 2(b), motivating support for asymmetric operation in the datapath.

The above findings narrow the practical design space to UE8M0 through UE4M4 without a PTS, and identify fractional scale formats such as UE5M3 and UE4M4 as the most promising candidates for the FP4 regime. The configurations in the retained space are further evaluated across four models and two datasets in Sec. 4 to assess the generalizability of the observed trends. However, fractional scales require a multiplier rather than a simple bit-shift, introducing a hardware cost that we account for in the datapath design presented next.

3.2. Datapath Template Implementation

To investigate how activation, weight and scale precision affect the hardware implementation, we propose a MAC datapath template. Fig. 3a shows the datapath. The pre-processor forms four products of operands which a shared reduction tree then sums. Alignment before the tree is performed against a pre-computed anchor position, which avoids comparing exponents across products (Lutz et al., 2024). A scale multiplier follows, and a bi-directional shifter aligns the partial result with the current scaled term through a carry-propagation adder (CPA). Then the accumulation result goes through a leading-zero detection (LZD) normalizer and round-ties-to-even (RNE) rounder (Rouhani et al., 2023a). The output after the LZD normalizer and rounder is written back to the accumulation register, which is read out again as the running sum for the next MAC cycle.

Prior MX-compatible designs focus on FP8 operands with E8M0 scale (İslamoğlu et al., 2025; Lutz et al., 2024). Instead, to enable our exploration into the MX-like design space, our proposed general hardware template is built on top of it with two innovations: ❶ When the scale factor is fractional and cannot be folded into the bi-directional shifter as a power-of-two, we implement an additional multiplier after the reduction tree. ❷ We parameterize the datapath on five format axes (eA,mA,eW,mW,mS\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{A}},\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}},\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{W}},\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{W}},\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{S}}), representing the exponent and mantissa widths of activations, weights, and shared scales11 1 The exponent size is eS=8−mS\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{S}}=8-\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{S}}, we also assume the activations and weights share the same scale type. The scale exponent eSe_{\mathrm{S}} is absent from the width chain because it enters only through the accumulator bi-directional shifter’s control path. and generate a datapath specialized to each configuration. A Chisel (Bachrach et al., 2012) generator evaluates those parameters at elaboration time and emits one RTL instance per design point. This parameterization absorbs asymmetric operand pairs and fractional scale, enabling a fair comparison of the hardware cost across the MX-like design space.

Table 2 gives each stage’s width as a function of these axes. These widths reveal two properties that drive the cost. First, the operand exponents set the tree width from both ends. The Anchor sits at the largest product magnitude, and the Sum-of-Product (SoP) field extends down to the smallest subnormal product (Es​u​bAE^{A}_{sub}, Es​u​bWE^{W}_{sub}). Wide-exponent formats therefore pay twice. Second, the scale multiplier inherits that same SoP width. The cost of a fractional scale is thus inseparable from the operand pair. Moreover, the MantAcc\mathrm{Mant}_{\mathrm{Acc}} appends a fixed significand of the partial result (e.g., 8 bits for BF16), which is independent of any format axis.

To make this concrete, consider E4M3 ×\times E2M1 with the UE6M2 scale. The activation E4M3 has maximum normal exponent EmaxA=8E^{A}_{\max}=8 and minimum EminA=−6\mathrm{E}^{\mathrm{A}}_{\min}=-6; the weight E2M1 has EmaxW=2\mathrm{E}^{\mathrm{W}}_{\max}=2 and EminW=0E^{W}_{\min}=0. So the largest possible product magnitude is 2.625×210≈211.42.625\times 2^{10}\approx 2^{11.4} (Rouhani et al., 2023a), placing its leading bit 11 positions above 202^{0} as the anchor; the smallest subnormal product 2−9×2−1=2−102^{-9}\times 2^{-1}=2^{-10} places its leading bit |Es​u​bA+Es​u​bW|=10\bigl|E^{A}_{sub}+E^{W}_{sub}\bigr|=10 positions below. Adding log2⁡N=2\log_{2}N=2 for four-way accumulation and a sign bit lifts the top to 2142^{14}, so the SoP field spans positions 2−102^{-10} through 2142^{14}, 25 bits in total. The scale multiplier then appends 2​(mS+1)+1=72(m_{S}+1)+1=7 bits for MantTerm=32\mathrm{Mant}_{\mathrm{Term}}=32, and the BF16 accumulator contributes a further 9 bits at the CPA for MantAcc=41\mathrm{Mant}_{\mathrm{Acc}}=41.

3.3. Automated Co-design Framework

The joint HW-SW DSE requires evaluating hundreds of quantization configurations, each demanding a matched hardware instance and a consistent software test setup. Performing this manually means hand-deriving the run-time values that define memory layout and dataflow mapping for every configuration, and manually keeping the software reference and hardware RTL in sync, a process that is both labor-intensive and error-prone at this scale. We therefore introduce an automated co-design flow that derives every downstream parameter, dataflow mapping, and RTL instance from a single design-time input, without manual calculation.

Our co-design flow builds on the SNAX platform (Antonio et al., 2025), an open-source RISC-V compute cluster in which a lightweight Snitch (Zaruba et al., 2021) core offloads computation to attached accelerators through Control and Status Register (CSR) instructions. As shown in Fig. 3b, a shared scratchpad memory and parameterized data streamers absorb the varying data widths across our DSE, while within the tensor core a CSR manager, a two-dimensional PE array with design-time configurable spatial parallelism, and a re-quantization unit carry out the MAC and format conversion.

Building on this platform, the flow is driven by a top-level orchestrator, as illustrated in Fig. 3c. The orchestrator takes a unified set of design-time parameters including operand datatypes, scale datatypes, workload dimension and tensor core dimension, and translates them into the configurations that feed the downstream flow. It then drives two parallel paths from this shared configuration. On the software compilation path, the orchestrator invokes data generation to produce quantized test data and software reference outputs by our custom quantization function, along with derivation of run-time CSR values for the target quantization configuration and workload to define the memory layout and computation dataflow. Together with a run-time library, this path yields a software binary. In parallel, the selected LLM is quantized by our custom quantizer and evaluated on the target dataset to obtain the accuracy benchmark. On the hardware generation path, the tensor core datapath is generated directly according to the orchestrator’s parameters, while the derived SNAX configuration, including the streamer width computed from the target bandwidth requirement, is fed into the SNAX toolchain to generate the surrounding components such as the streamers and CSR manager. Both steps use Chisel (Bachrach et al., 2012) to produce synthesizable HW RTL. The software binary and hardware RTL are then co-simulated to confirm that the generated hardware behaves consistently with the software reference. Separately, the RTL is synthesized to obtain area and power, which together with the accuracy benchmark form the inputs to the HW-SW co-analysis.

4. Experimental results

4.1. Experiment Setup

On the software side, we extend the open-source MX quantization library of microxcaling (Microsoft, 2023) and BitMoD (Chen et al., 2025) to produce identical numerical results matching the hardware datapath. We evaluate four language models: Qwen2.5-3B (Qwen Team, 2024), Qwen3-1.7B (Qwen Team, 2025), Llama-3.2-1B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma-3-1B (Gemma Team, 2025) on the full test split of WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) and 256 randomly sampled sequences of 2048 tokens from C4 (Raffel et al., 2020) to generalize our findings across datasets. Accuracy is measured as the perplexity degradation ΔPPL%\Delta\text{PPL}_{\%} as defined in Eq. (2).

On the hardware side, all generated designs are synthesized at 400 MHz with Synopsys Design Compiler on a TSMC 28 nm process, using standard cells at 0.8 V supply in the typical-typical corner. Power is estimated with Synopsys PrimeTime PX from the switching activity of a gate-level simulation over 2048 MAC operations to stabilize the average activity. At the system level, we instantiate a 4×\times16 PE array and its re-quantization units in the SNAX cluster (Yi et al., 2025) to capture the full tensor-core cost, driven by a 32×\times1024 tile of real weight and activation tensors from a representative transformer layer of Qwen2.5-3B (Qwen Team, 2024), whose distribution we observe to be consistent across layers. The reported area and power include the on-chip storage and data-movement overheads associated with asymmetric operand widths and fractional-scale metadata. Every configuration maps to the same 64-PE array at an easily achievable timing constraint of 400 MHz to ensure the minimum area across all designs and therefore sustains an identical throughput of 204.8 GOPS.

4.2. Accuracy Characterization

Building on observations in Sec. 3.1, we first evaluate the UE5M3–UE4M4 divergence and the limits of asymmetric precision across four models. The effect of scale format on accuracy depends critically on the target precision regime: it is negligible at high precision but becomes decisive once quantization is pushed aggressively. Taking A6W6 as representative of the high-precision regime, all four scale formats yield Δ\DeltaPPL% within a narrow 1.0–1.4% range across every model, as Fig. 4 shows, making the choice of scale format largely insensitive at this precision.

This changes sharply in the FP4 quantization regime. In the extreme A4W4 case, the coarse UE8M0 scale causes severe degradation, averaging 45.0%, while UE5M3, UE4M4 and NVFP4’s UE4M3 substantially outperform it, cutting average Δ\DeltaPPL% roughly in half. UE5M3 and UE4M4 further outperform UE4M3 by approximately 5 percentage points on average, by reclaiming the unused bit in the format, a gap that stems from Eq. (1). Yet the two are not interchangeable, since UE5M3 widens dynamic range while UE4M4 improves precision. Fig. 4 also shows that this divergence surfaces sharply on Qwen3-1.7B. Its late-layer activation outliers, once quantized to MXINT8, overflow UE4M4’s and UE4M3’s four-bit exponent range, causing a severe degradation, whereas UE5M3’s extended exponent range absorbs the same outliers and stays the more robust choice.

On top of scale format selection, asymmetric weight-activation quantization provides a further improvement, particularly pronounced in the FP4 regime, as anticipated by the distribution asymmetry noted in Sec. 3.1. Moving from A4W4 to asymmetric A6W4, which raises only the activation format to FP6, cuts Δ\DeltaPPL% across all four scale formats, nearly halving UE5M3’s degradation from 18.4% to 9.9% and UE4M4’s from 17.9% to 8.8%. Further raising activation precision to MXINT8 (A8W4) trims UE5M3’s degradation only slightly further, to 6.1%, while UE4M4 and UE4M3 instead rise to 16.0% and 19.2% due to their limited exponent range.

4.3. Hardware Cost Evaluation

In this subsection, we evaluate where an MX-like format spends its silicon cost, from the datapath stages up to the system level. We first break the datapath into stages across formats, as Fig. 5(a) shows. The accumulator is consistently the largest, holding 39–66% of the area. A fractional scale adds a scale-multiplier that reaches 36% and that a UE8M0 scale lacks, a cost traceable to Table 2, where the multiplier shares the accumulator’s MantTerm\mathrm{Mant}_{\mathrm{Term}} field.

We then fix the scale at UE8M0 and sweep operand pairs, tracking area and power against the aligned sum-of-products (SoP) width growing with e\mathrm{e} and m\mathrm{m} of operands, as shown in Fig. 5(b). Over SoP from 11 to 67 bits the MAC area grows 4.9×\times but power only 2.6×\times, since area follows the SoP width whereas power is set by actual switching in the multiplier and scatters against SoP. The fractional scale’s multiplier operates on this same SoP field, coupling its cost to the operand pair, as presented in Fig. 5(c). The heaviest scale, UE4M4, adds about 0.5×103​μ​m20.5\times 10^{3}\mu m^{2} on the narrow INT8×\timesE2M1 but 1.9×103​μ​m21.9\times 10^{3}\mu m^{2} on the wide E5M2×\timesE5M2, a 3.6×\times spread that no single design point reveals.

At the system level, where deployment budgets bind, these mechanisms pay off, as illustrated in Fig. 5(d). Of the 126 configurations, 60 draw both less area and power than the conventional symmetric-FP8 baseline, E4M3×\timesE4M3 with UE8M0, which uses 0.708​m​m20.708mm^{2} and 64.5​m​W64.5mW, and 30 of these are asymmetric with a fractional scale. A representative case, marked as a green star, is E2M3×\timesE2M1 with UE5M3, using 0.646​m​m20.646mm^{2} and 51.6​m​W51.6mW, 9% less area and 20% less power, while carrying a fractional scale the default lacks. However, the cost axis alone cannot decide which affordable format is worth adopting. The cost-only optimum, marked as a blue cross, is the FP4 pair at UE8M0, using 0.606​m​m20.606mm^{2} and 38.3​m​W38.3mW, and is ruled out by the accuracy characterization in Sec. 4.2.

4.4. Hardware–Software Co-analysis

We now bring accuracy and hardware cost together to locate the true Pareto-optimal configurations, using the joint HW-SW co-analysis in Fig. 6. Each point is one configuration of the MX-like space, its vertical position the mean Δ\DeltaPPL% across four models and its horizontal position the system-level cost, with every instance behind these points generated, verified, and synthesized by our automated co-design flow.

We find that the two single-sided conclusions each hold in exactly one precision regime. Above A6W6 the choice is dominated by hardware cost, as UE8M0 is Pareto-optimal, while a fractional scale buys no accuracy but adds up to +22% system power and +17% area over the UE8M0 baseline. The FP4 regime inverts this: the same UE4M4 scale now buys 27 percentage points of Δ\DeltaPPL  from 45.0% under UE8M0 down to 17.9%, while at FP4 operands the same fractional overhead falls to +4.6% area and +20.8% power. Within the fractional-scale family, UE5M3 emerges as the sweet spot, recovering 25.3% of Δ\DeltaPPL relative to the NVFP4-like UE4M3 at only +0.06% area and +0.49% power over that baseline, and showing more robustness than UE4M4, as discussed in Sec. 4.2. UE5M3 is therefore our recommended FP4 scale format.

We further mark three deployment thresholds in Fig. 6: 1) a 20 % perplexity-degradation budget, guided by comparisons with smaller unquantized models of the same families in our experiments, 2) a 60 mW power budget, corresponding to 3413 GOPS/W at our constant throughput which is close to the prior precision-scalable MX clusters in FP4 mode (Cuyckens et al., 2026), and 3) a 0.7 mm2 area budget, in line with prior MX systems at 0.59–0.60 mm2 on more advanced nodes (İslamoğlu et al., 2025; Cuyckens et al., 2026), with headroom at the 28 nm technology we use. Note that our conclusions are not tied to these specific values, and they hold for any accuracy threshold in 15–25% and any power budget in 56–64 mW. Within them, neither traditional baseline is feasible. Symmetric MXFP4 fails at 45.0% and the per-tensor-scale-free NVFP4-like UE4M3 configuration at 22.9%, while most feasible points are asymmetric, fractional-scale configurations that neither standard has defined before, led by A6W4 (E2M3×\timesE2M1) with UE5M3 scale.

This co-analysis lets a practitioner pick a configuration for their own accuracy and hardware budget, and points to which precision combinations future hardware should support as edge deployment evolves (Wang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026).

5. Conclusion

In this work, we characterize the previously unexplored joint accuracy-silicon Pareto frontier of the MX-like design space, spanned by scale format, weight format, and activation format. We define the full 8-bit scale format family jointly with asymmetric weight-activation precision, build a per-format specialized MAC datapath template for fair hardware cost evaluation across the space, and integrate both into an automated co-design flow on the open-source SNAX NPU platform. Our joint exploration shows that scale format is largely inconsequential above A6W6, where UE8M0 remains Pareto-optimal, but becomes decisive under FP4, where UE5M3 paired with asymmetric weight-activation precision reduces perplexity degradation by up to 25.3% relative to the NVFP4-like baseline with only a negligible hardware overhead.
